description: Cause and Effect is an analytical topic in Logical Reasoning. It involves studying two given statements to identify the cause-effect relationship between them.

sections.title: Basic Concepts
sections.description: To deeply understand this topic, it is essential to know the clear definitions of cause and effect and the difference between them.

key_concepts.explanation: The event or condition that gives rise to another event or prompts it to happen. Chronologically, the cause always occurs first.
The final event or reaction that occurs as a result of a cause. The effect always appears only after the cause has occurred.

sections.title: Types of Causes
sections.description: For analytical problem solving, causes are categorized based on their nature and their impact on events.

key_concepts.explanation: The event that occurred just before the effect and has a direct relationship with the outcome.
An event that is not linked to any other given event and is a separate cause on its own, having nothing to do with the other statement.
A hidden or indirect cause that simultaneously produces both the given statements as its effects (e.g., rain causing both waterlogging and traffic jams).

sections.title: Possible Cases in Questions
sections.description: In competitive exams, options are usually based on the following five standard cases, from which the correct one must be selected.

results: Statement I is the main cause.
Statement II is the direct effect of that cause.
Statement II is the main cause.
Statement I is the direct effect of that cause.
Both statements I and II are completely independent causes.
There is no cause-effect relationship between them.
Both statements I and II are effects of different independent causes.
Both statements I and II are effects of a single common cause.

sections.title: Steps to Solve Problems
sections.description: A systematic approach to establish the correct cause-effect relationship between the given statements.

steps.title: Analyze Statements
steps.detail: Carefully read both statements and understand what kind of event or situation they represent.

steps.title: Check Time Sequence
steps.detail: Determine which event would have logically or chronologically occurred first. The one that happens first is potentially the cause.

steps.title: Find Logical Connection
steps.detail: Ask yourself: 'Did the second event happen because of the first event?' If yes, there is a clear cause-effect relationship.

steps.title: Identify Independent Events
steps.detail: If there is no direct or scientific relation between the two events, check if they are linked by a third common cause, or if they are entirely independent.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.description: Common logical errors made by candidates while solving questions on this topic.

results: Just because two events happen simultaneously at the same time does not mean one is the cause of the other.
Mistakenly assuming the effect as the cause. Always remember that the cause exists before the effect in the timeline.
